## M1-E01 · Read the ER diagram

<details><summary>Hint 1 · direction</summary>

{'Read each line in both directions': 'one A has … B, and one B has … A.'}

</details>

<details><summary>Hint 2 · technique</summary>

"Zero to many" (circle + crow's foot) means the relationship is optional on that side.

</details>

<details><summary>Hint 3 · structure</summary>

## M1-E02 · Why not use the ISBN as the primary key?

<details><summary>Hint 1 · direction</summary>

The key is copied into every table that references it, so think about size.

</details>

<details><summary>Hint 2 · technique</summary>

What happens to a leading 0 when text becomes a number?

</details>

<details><summary>Hint 3 · structure</summary>

The alternative is a key the database makes up for you.

</details>

Final: [solution](../solutions/M1.md#m1-e02).

## M1-E03 · What does (23, 1) in authored mean?

<details><summary>Hint 1 · direction</summary>

`authored` holds only ids. Names live in `authors`, and titles live in `books`.

</details>

<details><summary>Hint 2 · technique</summary>

Look up id 23 in authors and id 1 in books.

</details>

<details><summary>Hint 3 · structure</summary>

`SELECT "title" FROM "books" WHERE "id" = 1;`

</details>

Final: [solution](../solutions/M1.md#m1-e03).

Two questions. What is the publisher's id? Which books have that id?

</details>

<details><summary>Hint 3 · structure</summary>

`SELECT "title" FROM "books" WHERE "publisher_id" = (SELECT "id" FROM "publishers" WHERE "publisher" = '...');`

{'The table is `publishers`, plural. The lecturer\'s first try failed with "no such table': 'publisher".'}

Find the id first, then the titles.

## M1-E06 · Average rating of In Memory of Memory

<details><summary>Hint 1 · direction</summary>

`ratings` has one row per rating, with a `book_id`.

</details>

<details><summary>Hint 2 · technique</summary>

The subquery finds the book's id (33 in the lecture).

</details>

<details><summary>Hint 3 · structure</summary>

`SELECT AVG("rating") FROM "ratings" WHERE "book_id" = (SELECT "id" FROM "books" WHERE "title" = 'In Memory of Memory');`

</details>

Final: [solution](../solutions/M1.md#m1-e06).

## M1-E07 · Who wrote The Birthday Party?

<details><summary>Hint 1 · direction</summary>

Start from what you know (the title) and walk to what you want (the name).

</details>

<details><summary>Hint 2 · technique</summary>

Three steps: book id → author_id (in authored) → name.

</details>

<details><summary>Hint 3 · structure</summary>

`SELECT "name" FROM "authors" WHERE "id" = (SELECT "author_id" FROM "authored" WHERE "book_id" = (SELECT "id" FROM "books" WHERE ...));`

</details>

Final: [solution](../solutions/M1.md#m1-e07).

## M1-E08 · Fernanda Melchor's books, with IN

<details><summary>Hint 1 · direction</summary>

The middle step returns *two* book ids.

</details>

<details><summary>Hint 2 · technique</summary>

`= (subquery)` is for exactly one value. For a list, use `IN (subquery)`.

</details>

<details><summary>Hint 3 · structure</summary>

`SELECT "title" FROM "books" WHERE "id" IN (SELECT "book_id" FROM "authored" WHERE "author_id" = (SELECT "id" FROM "authors" WHERE ...));`

</details>

Final: [solution](../solutions/M1.md#m1-e08).

## M1-E09 · Join sea lions to their migrations

<details><summary>Hint 1 · direction</summary>

JOIN puts a row of one table next to the matching row of another.

</details>

<details><summary>Hint 2 · technique</summary>

`ON` says which columns must be equal.

</details>

<details><summary>Hint 3 · structure</summary>

`SELECT * FROM "sea_lions" JOIN "migrations" ON "migrations"."id" = "sea_lions"."id";`

</details>

Final: [solution](../solutions/M1.md#m1-e09).

## M1-E10 · Keep every tracked sea lion (LEFT JOIN)

<details><summary>Hint 1 · direction</summary>

An OUTER join keeps unmatched rows and fills the gaps with NULL.

</details>

<details><summary>Hint 2 · technique</summary>

The table written first (before the JOIN keyword) is the "left" one.

</details>

<details><summary>Hint 3 · structure</summary>

`... FROM "sea_lions" LEFT JOIN "migrations" ON ...;`

</details>

Final: [solution](../solutions/M1.md#m1-e10).

## M1-E11 · Keep everything (FULL JOIN)

<details><summary>Hint 1 · direction</summary>

LEFT keeps the left side and RIGHT keeps the right side. What keeps both?

</details>

<details><summary>Hint 2 · technique</summary>

Missing values on either side become NULL.

</details>

<details><summary>Hint 3 · structure</summary>

`... FROM "sea_lions" FULL JOIN "migrations" ON ...;`

</details>

Final: [solution](../solutions/M1.md#m1-e11).

## M1-E12 · Let the column names decide (NATURAL JOIN)

<details><summary>Hint 1 · direction</summary>

A NATURAL JOIN matches every column whose name appears in both tables.

</details>

<details><summary>Hint 2 · technique</summary>

Both tables have a column named `id`.

</details>

<details><summary>Hint 3 · structure</summary>

`SELECT * FROM "sea_lions" NATURAL JOIN "migrations";`

</details>

Final: [solution](../solutions/M1.md#m1-e12).

## M1-E13 · Author names next to titles, with JOIN

<details><summary>Hint 1 · direction</summary>

The two entities are connected through `authored`.

</details>

<details><summary>Hint 2 · technique</summary>

Two JOINs, each matching a primary key with a foreign key.

</details>

<details><summary>Hint 3 · structure</summary>

`FROM "authors" JOIN "authored" ON "authors"."id" = "authored"."author_id" JOIN "books" ON ...`

</details>

Final: [solution](../solutions/M1.md#m1-e13).

## M1-E14 · Authors and translators in one list, labelled

<details><summary>Hint 1 · direction</summary>

Two queries with the same number of columns can be stacked with a set operator.

</details>

<details><summary>Hint 2 · technique</summary>

A literal `'author' AS "profession"` adds a constant column.

</details>

<details><summary>Hint 3 · structure</summary>

`SELECT 'author' AS "profession", "name" FROM "authors" UNION SELECT 'translator' AS "profession", "name" FROM "translators";`

</details>

Final: [solution](../solutions/M1.md#m1-e14).

## M1-E15 · Who is both an author and a translator?

<details><summary>Hint 1 · direction</summary>

This is the overlap of two sets.

</details>

<details><summary>Hint 2 · technique</summary>

`INTERSECT` between two SELECTs.

</details>

<details><summary>Hint 3 · structure</summary>

`SELECT "name" FROM "authors" INTERSECT SELECT "name" FROM "translators";`

</details>

Final: [solution](../solutions/M1.md#m1-e15).

## M1-E16 · Authors who are only authors

<details><summary>Hint 1 · direction</summary>

Take one set and remove another.

</details>

<details><summary>Hint 2 · technique</summary>

`EXCEPT`. The order of the two queries matters.

</details>

<details><summary>Hint 3 · structure</summary>

`SELECT "name" FROM "authors" EXCEPT SELECT "name" FROM "translators";`

</details>

Final: [solution](../solutions/M1.md#m1-e16).

## M1-E17 · Finish the lecture's query: the book Hughes and Jull Costa share

<details><summary>Hint 1 · direction</summary>

Each translator's book ids come from `translated` with a subquery for their translator id. Intersect the two lists.

</details>

<details><summary>Hint 2 · technique</summary>

Then wrap the whole INTERSECT inside `WHERE "id" IN (...)`.

</details>

<details><summary>Hint 3 · structure</summary>

`SELECT "title" FROM "books" WHERE "id" IN (SELECT "book_id" FROM "translated" WHERE "translator_id" = (...) INTERSECT SELECT "book_id" FROM "translated" WHERE "translator_id" = (...));`

</details>

Final: [solution](../solutions/M1.md#m1-e17).

## M1-E18 · Homework: in exactly one of the two sets

<details><summary>Hint 1 · direction</summary>

The two outer parts are (authors EXCEPT translators) and (translators EXCEPT authors).

</details>

<details><summary>Hint 2 · technique</summary>

Combine the two parts with UNION. Wrap each part in a subquery so that the set operators apply in the right order.

</details>

<details><summary>Hint 3 · structure</summary>

`SELECT "name" FROM (SELECT ... EXCEPT SELECT ...) UNION SELECT "name" FROM (SELECT ... EXCEPT SELECT ...);`

</details>

Final: [solution](../solutions/M1.md#m1-e18).

## M1-E19 · Average rating per book

<details><summary>Hint 1 · direction</summary>

`AVG("rating")` on its own averages the whole table (3.84 here). You need one average per book.

</details>

<details><summary>Hint 2 · technique</summary>

Group the rows by the book they belong to.

</details>

<details><summary>Hint 3 · structure</summary>

`SELECT "book_id", ROUND(AVG("rating"), 2) AS "average rating" FROM "ratings" GROUP BY "book_id";`

</details>

Final: [solution](../solutions/M1.md#m1-e19).

## M1-E20 · Only the well-rated books (HAVING)

<details><summary>Hint 1 · direction</summary>

WHERE filters rows before grouping. Which keyword filters groups?

</details>

<details><summary>Hint 2 · technique</summary>

`HAVING` comes after GROUP BY, and `ORDER BY` comes last.

</details>

<details><summary>Hint 3 · structure</summary>

`... GROUP BY "book_id" HAVING "average rating" > 4.0 ORDER BY "average rating" DESC;`

</details>

Final: [solution](../solutions/M1.md#m1-e20).

## M1-E21 · How many ratings per book?

<details><summary>Hint 1 · direction</summary>

Same grouping as before, with a different aggregate.

</details>

<details><summary>Hint 2 · technique</summary>

`COUNT("rating")` counts the rows in each group.

</details>

<details><summary>Hint 3 · structure</summary>

`SELECT "book_id", COUNT("rating") FROM "ratings" GROUP BY "book_id";`

</details>

Final: [solution](../solutions/M1.md#m1-e21).

## D1-01 · Joined on the wrong column

<details><summary>Hint 1 · direction</summary>

Read each ON clause aloud. Does it connect a primary key to the matching foreign key?

</details>

<details><summary>Hint 2 · technique</summary>

`authors.id` is an *author* id. Which column of `authored` holds author ids?

</details>

<details><summary>Hint 3 · structure</summary>

The first ON should use `authored.author_id`.

</details>

Final: [solution](../solutions/M1.md#d1-01).

## D1-02 · Duplicate rows from a one-to-many join

<details><summary>Hint 1 · direction</summary>

How many rows of `ratings` match one book?

</details>

<details><summary>Hint 2 · technique</summary>

A JOIN outputs one row per *matching pair*, so a book with 20 ratings appears 20 times.

</details>

<details><summary>Hint 3 · structure</summary>

Collapse the duplicates with `DISTINCT` or `GROUP BY "books"."id"`, or use `WHERE "id" IN (SELECT "book_id" FROM "ratings")`.

</details>

Final: [solution](../solutions/M1.md#d1-02).

## D1-03 · One average instead of one per book

<details><summary>Hint 1 · direction</summary>

Without grouping, an aggregate collapses the *whole table* into one row.

</details>

<details><summary>Hint 2 · technique</summary>

Which column defines "per book"?

</details>

<details><summary>Hint 3 · structure</summary>

Add `GROUP BY "book_id"`.

</details>

Final: [solution](../solutions/M1.md#d1-03).

## D1-04 · `=` with a subquery that returns many rows

<details><summary>Hint 1 · direction</summary>

How many rows does the middle subquery return?

</details>

<details><summary>Hint 2 · technique</summary>

`= (subquery)` in SQLite silently uses only the **first** row.

</details>

<details><summary>Hint 3 · structure</summary>

Use the set-membership operator.

</details>

Final: [solution](../solutions/M1.md#d1-04).

## D1-05 · Grouped by the wrong column

<details><summary>Hint 1 · direction</summary>

Each group becomes one output row. How many distinct ids are there?

</details>

<details><summary>Hint 2 · technique</summary>

Group by what you want one row *per*.

</details>

<details><summary>Hint 3 · structure</summary>

`GROUP BY "year"`

</details>

Final: [solution](../solutions/M1.md#d1-05).

The error message names the problem precisely.

## D1-07 · WHERE on an aggregate

<details><summary>Hint 1 · direction</summary>

WHERE runs before rows are grouped. Does the average exist at that point?

</details>

<details><summary>Hint 2 · technique</summary>

Conditions on groups use a different keyword.

</details>

<details><summary>Hint 3 · structure</summary>

Move the condition into `HAVING`, after GROUP BY.

<details><summary>Hint 1 · direction</summary>

What happens to a row with no match in an INNER JOIN?

</details>

<details><summary>Hint 2 · technique</summary>

You want every row of the table written first.

</details>

<details><summary>Hint 3 · structure</summary>

`LEFT JOIN`

</details>

Final: [solution](../solutions/M1.md#d1-08).

<details><summary>Hint 1 · direction</summary>

Compare the number of columns on each side.

</details>

<details><summary>Hint 2 · technique</summary>

Set operators stack rows, so every row must have the same shape.

<details><summary>Hint 3 · structure</summary>

Select the same columns on both sides, here just `"name"`.
